title: Chemistry Basics · Episode 1
chapters: Solid, liquid, gas … and stranger things

units.t: Chemistry Basics. Episode one.
In this episode: What atoms are made of, Solid, liquid, gas … and stranger things, The periodic table and Carbon: the element of everything.
Part one. What atoms are made of.
Everything you can touch is made of atoms, and atoms are almost entirely empty space.
Atoms are real.
The Greek thinker Democritus proposed around 400 BC that matter is made of tiny, uncuttable particles; atomos means 'uncuttable'.
For two thousand years this stayed a guess, and Aristotle's view that matter is continuous won out.
Around 1808, English chemist John Dalton revived the idea with evidence: elements combine in fixed proportions by weight, which made sense if they came in discrete units.
Even then, many scientists treated atoms as a handy bookkeeping device.
In 1905, Albert Einstein explained Brownian motion, the jittery dance of tiny particles in water, giving strong evidence that atoms really exist.
Jean Perrin's experiments soon confirmed it.
Tiny, with a core.
Atoms are roughly 0.
1 to 0.
5 nanometres across; a nanometre is a millionth of a millimetre.
Hundreds of thousands of carbon atoms side by side would just span a human hair, and one grain of table salt holds around a billion billion atoms.
Light microscopes cannot show them, because atoms are smaller than the wavelength of visible light.
In 1989, IBM researchers spelled out their logo with 35 xenon atoms.
J.
J.
Thomson discovered the electron in 1897.
Around 1909, Geiger and Marsden, working under New Zealand-born Ernest Rutherford, fired alpha particles at gold foil; a few bounced almost straight back.
In 1911 Rutherford concluded that atoms have a tiny, dense, positive nucleus.
James Chadwick found its neutral neutrons in 1932.
Mostly empty space.
If an atom were the size of a football stadium, the nucleus would be about the size of a pea.
More than 99.
9% of an atom's mass sits in that nucleus, while nearly all its volume is space where electrons might be found.
Quantum physics describes electrons as fuzzy clouds of probability, not tiny planets on neat orbits.
So why can't your hand pass through a table?
Electrons repel other electrons, and a quantum rule called the Pauli exclusion principle stops them crowding into the same state.
When you 'touch' something, your atoms never actually touch the object's atoms.
What you feel is electromagnetic repulsion across a tiny gap.
Elements and isotopes.
Every atom with one proton is hydrogen; six protons, carbon; eight, oxygen; 79, gold.
That count, the atomic number, fixes the element.
Atoms of one element can carry different numbers of neutrons.
These versions, called isotopes, behave almost identically in chemistry but differ in mass and stability.
Carbon-12 makes up about 99% of natural carbon.
Carbon-14 is radioactive: its unstable nucleus breaks down by releasing a beta particle, other isotopes release alpha particles or gamma rays.
Each radioactive isotope has a half-life, the time for half a sample to decay.
Carbon-14's is about 5,730 years, which allows radiocarbon dating of once-living material up to about 50,000 years old.
Uranium-238's is about 4.
5 billion years, which helps date rocks and the Earth.
Many smoke alarms contain a trace of americium-241.
Electrons and quarks.
Chemistry is mostly about electrons.
Atoms are most stable with a full outer shell, so they share, give away or take electrons to form bonds.
Sodium readily gives up its single outer electron and chlorine readily takes one, forming table salt.
Carbon, with four outer electrons, shares them in long chains and rings, forming the backbone of every living thing.
Helium's shell is already full, so it barely reacts, making it safe for party balloons.
Deeper still, protons and neutrons are made of quarks, bound by the strong force.
A proton has two 'up' quarks and one 'down'; a neutron has one up and two down.
Electrons, as far as we know, are not made of anything smaller.
The key idea: The idea of atoms is ancient, but solid evidence came only in the last two centuries.
Part two. Solid, liquid, gas … and stranger things.
School taught us three states of matter.
Nature has more, including one that fills the stars and one that was only made in a lab in 1995.
Particles on the move.
Everything is made of atoms and molecules that never stop moving.
In a solid, they are locked in place and can only vibrate, which is why a brick keeps its shape.
In a liquid, they are still packed closely but can slide past one another, so water takes the shape of its container.
In a gas, they fly about freely, bouncing off each other and the walls, with mostly empty space between them.
The molecules in the air you are breathing travel at roughly 500 metres per second, faster than a passenger jet, colliding with each other billions of times every second.
Changing state.
Heat a solid and its particles vibrate harder until they break out of their fixed places and it melts.
Keep heating and some escape as a gas.
While ice melts, its temperature stays at 0°C, because the energy goes into breaking the bonds holding particles in place rather than making them move faster.
Boiling also depends on the air pressure above.
Water boils at 100°C at sea level but only around 70°C on the summit of Mount Everest, which makes a decent cup of tea surprisingly hard.
Some substances skip the liquid stage.
Dry ice, which is frozen carbon dioxide, turns straight into gas, a change called sublimation.
Glass and pitch.
Glass has jumbled atoms like a liquid yet is rigid, so scientists call it an amorphous solid.
The story that old windows are thicker at the bottom because glass flowed over centuries is a myth.
Old panes were spun or blown unevenly, and glaziers often fitted the thick edge down.
At room temperature, glass would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag visibly.
Pitch, a tar-like substance that shatters under a hammer, truly flows.
In 1927 Professor Thomas Parnell at the University of Queensland poured heated pitch into a funnel and, three years later, cut its stem open.
A drop takes the best part of a decade to fall, and fewer than a dozen have.
A camera set up in 2000 failed at the crucial moment.
Plasma and condensates.
Heat a gas enough and collisions knock electrons off their atoms.
The result is plasma, a mix of free electrons and positive ions that conducts electricity and responds strongly to magnetic fields.
Lightning, neon signs, auroras and every star, including the Sun, are plasma, so most of the ordinary visible matter in the universe is thought to be in this state.
At the other extreme, Bose and Einstein predicted in the 1920s that atoms cooled near absolute zero would fall into one quantum state and act as a single giant wave.
In 1995 Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman in Colorado cooled rubidium atoms to around 170 billionths of a degree above absolute zero and made one.
They shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics with Wolfgang Ketterle.
The in-betweens.
Mix cornflour with water and you get oobleck, a goo that pours like a liquid but turns firm when you punch it or run across it.
Scientists call it a non-Newtonian fluid, because its thickness changes with the force applied.
Liquid crystals flow like a liquid but line up in an orderly way like a crystal, and turning them with electric fields is how many screens control light.
Sand and grain can pour through a funnel like water, yet hold up a person standing on a beach.
Nature is under no obligation to follow the labels people invented.
The key idea: Solids, liquids and gases differ in how freely their particles move.
Part three. The periodic table.
One chart organises every element in the universe, and when it was invented, it predicted elements nobody had found yet.
A bold gamble.
By the 1860s, chemists knew about 60 elements but had no pattern linking them.
Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev wrote each element's properties on cards and arranged them by atomic weight, grouping similar behaviour in columns.
Legend says the answer came in a dream.
His crucial move was boldness: he left gaps for undiscovered elements and described them, calling them eka-aluminium, eka-silicon and eka-boron.
Gallium, 1875, scandium, 1879, and germanium, 1886, matched his predictions closely.
When gallium's first density disagreed, he suggested the sample was impure, and a remeasurement proved him right.
Today the table is ordered by atomic number, the count of protons, as Henry Moseley showed in 1913 using X-rays.
Rows and columns.
Each row, or period, begins a new shell of electrons, and the table has seven periods.
Each column, or group, holds elements with the same number of outer electrons, which is why they behave alike.
Group 1, the alkali metals such as sodium and potassium, are so reactive they are stored under oil and fizz or explode in water.
Group 17, the halogens such as fluorine and chlorine, are highly reactive non-metals; chlorine compounds disinfect swimming pools.
Group 18, the noble gases helium, neon and argon, barely react at all.
Argon makes up almost 1% of the air you breathe.
Metals and the middle.
More than three-quarters of elements are metals: usually shiny, good conductors, and easy to hammer or draw into wire.
Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature.
Non-metals such as carbon, oxygen and the halogens cluster on the right.
Between them, the metalloids silicon and germanium have mixed properties; silicon's controllable electrical behaviour underpins computer chips.
The wide central block holds the transition metals, including iron, copper, gold and platinum, many making coloured compounds and useful catalysts.
The lanthanides, with scandium and yttrium, are the rare earths.
Most aren't especially rare, just hard to find in concentrated, mineable deposits.
Neodymium makes powerful magnets for wind turbines and electric cars, and Australia mines rare earths at Mount Weld in Western Australia.
Names and new elements.
Some symbols reveal Latin names: Na for sodium, natrium, K for potassium, kalium, Fe for iron, ferrum, Au for gold, aurum, Pb for lead, plumbum, which gives us 'plumber'.
The Swedish village of Ytterby lent its name to four elements.
Curium, einsteinium and mendelevium honour scientists.
IUPAC approves new names.
Almost all elements up to uranium, 92, occur naturally; technetium and promethium are found only in tiny traces.
Heavier ones are made by smashing atoms together.
Element 118, oganesson, completed the seventh row, named in 2016 with nihonium, moscovium and tennessine.
Superheavy atoms last milliseconds or less.
Physicists suspect an 'island of stability' where some might last longer, and labs are chasing elements 119 and 120.
Made in stars.
Hydrogen, helium and a little lithium formed in the first few minutes after the Big Bang, about 13.
8 billion years ago.
Stars then fuse lighter elements into heavier ones, building carbon, oxygen and more up to iron, where fusion stops releasing energy.
Elements heavier than iron form mainly in extreme events, such as supernova explosions and collisions between neutron stars.
A neutron star merger observed in 2017 was seen producing heavy elements, probably including gold and platinum.
The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made inside stars that died before the Sun was born.
As Carl Sagan put it, we are made of star stuff.
The key idea: Mendeleev's table left gaps for undiscovered elements, and their predicted properties proved right.
Part four. Carbon: the element of everything.
The same atom makes a diamond, a pencil, a soccer-ball-shaped molecule and most of you.
Carbon's secret is its talent for holding hands.
The great connector.
Each carbon atom has four electrons available for bonding, so it can link with up to four other atoms.
Crucially, it bonds strongly with other carbon atoms, forming long chains, branches and rings that act as frameworks for other elements.
That flexibility makes carbon the backbone of proteins, fats, sugars and DNA.
The chemistry of carbon compounds is so vast that it has its own branch, organic chemistry, covering many millions of known substances.
Carbon is common too.
After hydrogen, helium and oxygen, it is the fourth most abundant element in the universe by mass, and it makes up around a fifth of your body by mass.
Born in stars.
The Big Bang produced almost no carbon.
It is forged inside stars, where three helium nuclei fuse into one carbon nucleus.
In the early 1950s, the British astronomer Fred Hoyle realised that by the known physics this reaction should be far too rare to make the carbon we see.
Since carbon obviously exists, he reasoned, carbon nuclei must have a particular energy state that made the reaction much more likely.
In 1953 he persuaded sceptical experimental physicists at Caltech to look for it, and they found it close to where he had predicted.
The carbon in your cells was made this way, in stars that lived and died long before the Sun formed.
Diamond, graphite and ‘lead’.
In diamond, each carbon atom is locked to four neighbours in a rigid 3D framework, making it the hardest natural material known.
Natural diamonds form over a hundred kilometres down in the mantle, under enormous heat and pressure, and rise in rare volcanic eruptions.
In graphite, atoms bond to three neighbours in flat hexagon sheets, stacked like pages and held together weakly, so they slide and graphite is soft and slippery.
At the surface graphite is more stable, so diamonds are technically turning into it, far too slowly to notice.
Pencils contain no lead.
A pure graphite deposit found at Borrowdale, England, in the sixteenth century looked like lead ore, so it was called black lead.
Pencil ‘lead’ is graphite mixed with clay: more clay makes a harder H pencil, more graphite a softer B pencil.
Buckyballs and graphene.

In 1985, Harold Kroto, Robert Curl and Richard Smalley blasted graphite with a laser and found a stable molecule of exactly 60 carbon atoms: a hollow sphere of 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons, like a soccer ball.
They named it buckminsterfullerene, after Buckminster Fuller's geodesic domes, or buckyball.
The three shared the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Buckyballs have since been detected in space.
Graphene is a single sheet of graphite, one atom thick.
In 2004 at the University of Manchester, Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov pressed sticky tape onto graphite and kept peeling flakes until some were one atom thick.
Graphene is strong, flexible, nearly transparent and conducts well.
They won the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
Carbon on the move.
The carbon in your body has been on a long journey.
Plants pull carbon dioxide from the air and use sunlight to build it into sugars.
Animals eat the plants, and both release carbon dioxide as they breathe and decay.
The oceans absorb vast amounts of carbon dioxide, and over millions of years carbon is locked away in limestone and other rocks, then slowly returned by volcanoes.
Fossil fuels such as coal, oil and gas are the remains of ancient living things, carbon buried and stored for millions of years.
Burning them releases that carbon into the air far faster than natural processes can remove it, which is the main reason carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere are rising.
The key idea: Carbon forms four strong bonds, so it can build the chains and rings that underpin the molecules of life.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What finally turned atoms from a useful idea into accepted fact?
Answer. Evidence from chemistry and from jittery particles in water.
Question two. In which state are particles packed closely but able to slide past one another?
Answer. Liquid.
Question three. Why did Mendeleev's table convince chemists it reflected something real?
Answer. It predicted unknown elements that were later found.
Question four. Why is carbon the backbone of the molecules of life?
Answer. It forms strong bonds that build chains and rings.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
